title: 石匠与搬运工
text:
Stone is awkward cargo even before it becomes part of a wall. The workshop contains samples and tools, but the weight lies at the quarry, and the place where the stone is needed stands beyond a bridge. A mason can mark the right slab and judge how it should sit; a porter knows how to make a load stay on a cart without cracking an edge. Neither skill replaces the other. Their shared errand begins in the workshop because the choice of blocks must precede loading. The quarry follows, not as a picturesque stop but as the place where the material can be selected and lifted. The site is the point at which the cargo becomes building work.

The bridge matters because a cart carrying stone cannot pass every narrow lane. An empty cart is easier to turn, yet it still has to be taken somewhere after the load is delivered. The warehouse provides a place to record what has come in and what has gone out. An inn by the bridge serves another kind of business: a builder can discuss tomorrow's work there without bringing the whole crew back to the site. These places may stand close to one another on a map, but the reasons for visiting them are distinct. A record of masonry that lists only the completed wall would hide the journeys needed to bring one slab to it.

Raffaele the mason and Ivo the porter meet at the workshop before the first bell and select blocks of stone. Together they take a cart to the quarry, where Raffaele marks a slab and Ivo loads it. The cart brings them to a building site beyond the bridge, a journey of forty minutes. There Raffaele sets the slab in a wall while Ivo unloads the remaining stone. After they eat a brief meal on the site, Ivo drives the empty cart to the warehouse and records the delivery. Raffaele goes on foot to an inn by the bridge to discuss the next day's work with the builder.

The two workers share the same route through the site, and they share a brief meal there, but the work performed at the site is divided. One sets the slab in a wall; the other unloads the remaining stone. After the meal their paths separate. The porter drives the cart to the warehouse and records the delivery. The mason walks to the inn to talk about the next day's task. It would be tempting to give both men the cart because it has appeared in their common journey; the final sentences rule that out for the mason. The account says he goes on foot.

One passage has a stated length: the cart's journey from the quarry to the site takes forty minutes. No such number is supplied for the initial cart trip, for the porter's later drive, or for the mason's walk. The meal at the site is described as brief, but that word belongs to eating, not to travel. This distinction matters in reconstructing labor. Time spent carrying a slab across a bridge is part of the cost of making a wall, while time spent fitting it into place is another. The route is shared long enough to make the two jobs interdependent and then breaks into different obligations.

Stone does not become a wall merely by reaching a site. It must be chosen, lifted, carried without damage, unloaded, and set where a builder has planned for it. The porter and mason share responsibility for the material but not the same final appointment. One follows the empty cart and its account of delivery; the other follows a conversation about work still to come. The meal on the site briefly gathers them before those obligations pull apart. The forty-minute cart passage is a conspicuous span of the day, yet much of the labor around it resists any simple reckoning in minutes.

title: 洗衣妇的往返
text:
Clothing arrives at a washerwoman's kitchen in a condition that its owner would rather forget. Every piece has to be sorted before water is used. Heavy cloth takes one treatment, a delicate sleeve another; a stain on a merchant's shirt may demand more attention than a whole bundle of plain linen. The kitchen is the beginning of the work because it offers a table and a place to inspect what has been entrusted to her. The river steps supply water and room for rinsing, but they do not offer the privacy of home. Other people wash nearby, and the condition of a garment is visible to them. A meadow outside the gate provides open air for drying, at the price of another journey with damp weight.

The bundle changes as it moves. It is dirty when carried to the river, wet when taken toward the meadow, and clean but still vulnerable to dust when put onto the handcart. A merchant paying for washing wants the clothes returned, not merely cleaned somewhere beyond his sight. The house where they are delivered is therefore a necessary stop in the chain. The woman does not finish her own day at that doorway. A torn sleeve remains to be mended, and her kitchen receives her again as a place of work rather than as a place of rest.

At dawn Bianca, a washerwoman, sorts a merchant household's clothes in her own kitchen. She carries the bundle on foot to the river steps and washes it there for three hours. Bianca then goes to a meadow outside the gate and hangs the cloth to dry. In the afternoon she gathers it and takes a handcart to the merchant's house, where she delivers the clean clothes. Before supper she walks back to her kitchen and mends a torn sleeve.

There is a duration for washing: three hours at the river steps. Nothing in that phrase measures the walk there. The return to the kitchen is explicitly a walk, and the delivery to the merchant is made with a handcart. The route to the meadow is described without a mode or a number of minutes. This mixture of exact and absent detail is ordinary in accounts of work. People remembered the weight of the washing and the hours it occupied more readily than the length of each lane they crossed. A faithful route can preserve what is known while leaving the other intervals empty.

The repetition of the kitchen at the start and end is especially revealing. Were one to keep only a list of places, the two visits might collapse into one. The first contains sorting; the last contains mending. Between them lie washing, drying, and delivery. The tasks are ordered by what cloth needs next, not by a clock imposed from outside. Rain might interrupt the meadow, a buyer might call before all the clothes are dry, and another household might send an urgent bundle. None of those possible changes occurs in the stated day, so they do not belong to this woman's marked chain. What remains is a particular sequence, not every errand her occupation could have required.

By the time the clean clothes reach the merchant's door, the river water has left them and the meadow air has done its part. The owner may notice only whether the fabric is clean and whole. A washerwoman notices the altered weight of the bundle, the strain of lifting wet cloth, and the sleeve that still needs a stitch. Her return to the kitchen does not undo the delivery; it begins another modest task in the same room where the day opened. The repeated kitchen gives the route its shape without making the work circular in purpose. The meadow and the river are open working spaces, exposed to weather and to the notice of strangers. The kitchen is sheltered, but it contains obligations no less exacting: sorting before the journey and mending after it. The woman carries those duties between the two kinds of space.

title: 公证人的文书
text:
A notary's papers appear light beside stone or grain, yet moving them through a town can occupy most of a day. A contract copied in an office has to be witnessed, compared with other records, and sometimes taken to the place whose boundary it describes. The office near the square is where the words are prepared and later sealed. The guild hall supplies people whose signatures give the contract a public form. The customs house holds a register that may confirm a disputed entry. A vineyard outside the walls is different from all three: its visible ground gives meaning to lines on a page. The notary's route follows the demands of proof, not the shortest way past interesting buildings.

The work is punctuated by waiting and reading. A clerk can send a visitor onward, but the visitor must still find the right register and spend time with it. Such time is easily confused with the journey that came before it. The crossing of the bridge has a measured length; the reading at the customs house has another. The hired horse appears only after the register has been consulted. No one needs to assume that the horse carried the notary across the bridge simply because it appears later in the account.

Carlo the notary opens his office near the square and copies a contract while the shops are still shuttered. At the morning bell he walks to the cloth guild hall, where he witnesses two signatures. A clerk sends him onward to the customs house. Carlo crosses the bridge in eighteen minutes and checks a cargo register there. He spends half an hour reading the register, then rides a hired horse to a vineyard outside the walls to record a boundary agreement. At dusk he returns to his office by horse and seals the day's papers.

The vineyard visit makes the route leave the town's paper offices for a place where a boundary can be described in relation to vines, walls, and paths. It is still a notarial activity, not farm labor. When the notary returns at dusk, his office has become the setting for sealing what the earlier visits allowed him to write. The repeated place carries a new task. The day's route thus forms a loop from office to guild hall, customs house, vineyard, and office again. The loop is not a single journey of known duration. It is a sequence of activities with different means of travel in between.

The account is precise about eighteen minutes for a bridge crossing and half an hour for reading the register. It is less precise about the ride to the vineyard and the ride home. A map might suggest a distance, but no map can turn the absence of a stated time into a measured value. The distinction between a place where a document is signed and a place where it is checked also matters. If every stop were labeled simply 'paperwork,' the order of the notary's labor would be lost. The contract becomes useful through several different actions, and the notary must be placed at each site where those actions occur.

A boundary written on a page may be neat where the ground itself is irregular. That is why the final outward visit leads past the walls to vines rather than to another desk. In town the notary's authority depends on a signature, a register, and a seal; outside it depends also on what can be seen and named. These forms of evidence do not appear all at once. They are gathered in an order, and the notary carries the accumulating account back to his office. Dusk closes the writing day, though nothing here tells how long every ride has been. Paper keeps an orderly version of events, while the streets require turns, waits, and changes of conveyance. The notary's route joins those different kinds of order. A seal at dusk can close the written matter only because the necessary people and places were reached earlier.

title: 梳羊毛的母女
text:
Wool passes through many hands before it can become clothing. Carding makes a tangled basket of fleece ready for the finer work that follows, and a household that cards wool may depend on others to dye, spin, or weave it. The courtyard at home is large enough for mother and daughter to work together when rain keeps the streets quiet. The dyer's yard offers scales and a place to agree on weight. The public oven supplies warmth and an ordinary meal without requiring either worker to abandon the day's errands. None of these places belongs to one trade alone. Courtyards, ovens, and markets gather people whose work intersects for a few hours and then separates.

The daughter is old enough to take a small bundle through the streets herself. Her hope of learning finer work gives the convent gate a purpose that differs from her mother's bargaining at the wool market. The route to the gate takes a measured ten minutes. No such duration is given for the mother's trip, though the market is named. One might suppose that both women use the same street for a time after their meal, but the account says only that they go to different destinations. A chain should follow what the narrative supports rather than what a plausible street plan invites.

On a rainy morning, Agata the wool carder and her daughter Fiore card a basket of fleece at home. When the sky clears, they carry the fleece to the dyer's courtyard and weigh it. They next walk to the public oven, where they eat bread and cheese. After the meal Agata goes alone to the wool market to bargain for more fleece. Fiore instead walks to the convent gate, a trip of ten minutes, and delivers a small bundle of spun yarn. She is sixteen and hopes to learn finer work.

Their common morning has three stages. First comes carding at home, where the fleece is handled. Next comes weighing in the dyer's courtyard, where it is judged as a quantity. Then comes bread and cheese at the oven, a modest break before more work. The meal is an activity at the oven, not a journey to it; the journey is the walk described in the same sentence. The two later errands branch from this shared stop. The mother seeks additional fleece and must bargain for it. The daughter delivers yarn, which belongs to a different stage of production from the fleece they carded together.

It is possible to tell this as the story of one household without losing the separate persons inside it. Mother and daughter rely on each other's labor, but one should not be assigned the other's final destination. Nor should the daughter's age be treated as an activity or a time stamp. It describes the person who undertakes the convent errand. The weather supplies another kind of timing. Rain delays the departure until the sky clears, yet it does not give a number of minutes for the wait. Such distinctions let a short account preserve the shape of a working day: shared labor, a common meal, and two routes that end in different forms of exchange.

A basket of wool looks much the same at the start and end of a street, but its meaning changes with each hand that receives it. At home it is work to be carded; in the dyer's yard it is weight to be judged; at market it becomes a possible purchase. Yarn at the convent gate belongs to a later stage, finer and more portable. The daughter's hope for such work is part of the family's economy, even though it is not measured in today's sale. The shared meal stands between common labor and these different prospects. The daughter's small parcel and the mother's hoped-for purchase face different futures. One carries completed yarn outward; the other seeks new raw fleece. Their shared morning makes those futures possible, but it does not make the destinations the same.

title: 园丁送菜
text:
A garden behind a wall may look like a retreat from the busy parts of a town, but the vegetables grown there are tied to kitchens beyond it. Beans have to be gathered while their pods are useful, not when a cart happens to be free. Herbs demand another sort of attention: a small cutting may lose its scent if it is crushed under the weight of the main harvest. The palace kitchen orders both sorts of produce, yet they do not necessarily arrive in one load. A gardener who has delivered beans can be sent out again for rosemary that was not mentioned when the first basket was packed. The route of a working day follows such changes in demand.

The handcart is suited to a heavy basket on streets broad enough for its wheels. Near the herb plot, beyond the mill, a person can choose a handful of stems without returning with the same vehicle. The mill itself is a landmark rather than a stop for grinding in this account. It helps locate the plot, but the gardener has no stated activity inside it. The palace kitchen, on the other hand, is visited twice for different deliveries. A list of unique places would reduce those visits to one and conceal the cook's second request. Home appears at the end as a site where tools must be cleaned before they can be used again.

Before the heat rises, Saverio the gardener gathers beans in a walled garden behind the house. He loads them onto a handcart and pushes it to the palace kitchen, where he delivers the first basket. The cook asks for herbs as well. Saverio walks to the herb plot beyond the mill and cuts rosemary there for half an hour. He then walks back to the palace kitchen, a journey of twenty-five minutes, and delivers the herbs. Late in the day he goes home on foot and cleans his tools.

The difference between cutting and traveling is unusually clear. The rosemary is cut for half an hour at the herb plot. The walk back to the kitchen takes twenty-five minutes. These are two durations attached to different parts of the day. One cannot make the return journey half an hour long simply because the cutting took that long, nor can the time of the walk be used as the length of the garden work. The other journeys have no stated measure. The first is made with a handcart, the movement to the herb plot is a walk, and the last return home is on foot.

The palace's demand reaches into a small walled garden and draws a worker through several different settings. There is gathering, a delivery, cutting, another delivery, and cleaning. Each stop has a local purpose. The work is linked by vegetables and herbs, but the gardener's path is not a straight line from plot to customer. It bends out toward another source and back to the same kitchen. This pattern is easy to miss if one reads only for the final meal that the ingredients will make possible. The meal is not described as an activity of the gardener, who remains concerned with supplying and preparing his tools.

The palace kitchen is a demanding customer because it can change its mind after the first basket has arrived. The gardener's response is visible in the bend of his route. He does not remain at the kitchen to argue about the omission; he goes back out for the herb that has become necessary. The mill on the way to the plot is passed rather than used, while the plot itself supplies a short period of cutting. A small bundle of rosemary may appear less burdensome than the beans, yet it costs a separate walk. When he reaches home, the cleaning of tools shows that another growing day is already being prepared. Soil on a blade can spoil its edge, and a cart left in the street can hinder a neighbor. The route through garden, kitchen, herb plot, kitchen, and home is a working circuit with a second delivery at its center, not a simple procession from producer to consumer.

title: 纺线后的差事
text:
A spinner's thread can be carried in a small bundle, but it carries many hours of work with it. A wheel in a courtyard turns while household sounds pass in and out: a door opening, water set down, voices from a neighboring room. The thread finished there is not yet cloth. Its price has to be agreed with a weaver, whose shop stands away from the courtyard. That agreement is an activity in its own right, not simply the end of a walk. From the shop the day continues toward a fountain and a relative's house. The purposes of these places differ so sharply that the same basket cannot explain them all.

The market fountain is a public source of water and a meeting place, but the account uses it in a narrow way. A jug is filled there. It is then carried to an aunt's house, where a meal is prepared. The aunt's visit lasts an hour. No journey in the story is said to last an hour. The spinner is on foot when she takes the thread to the weaver, walks to the fountain, and makes her last return. The manner of the shorter passage with the jug is described by the act of carrying it, without a further measured time.

Caterina, a spinner, sits at her wheel in the courtyard after breakfast and finishes a length of thread. She takes the thread on foot to the weaver's shop and agrees on its price. By noon she walks to the market fountain and fills a jug. She carries the jug to her aunt's house, where she stays for an hour and helps prepare a meal. The visit ends before the evening bell. Caterina then walks back to the courtyard and sets the empty basket beside her wheel.

The chain returns to the courtyard with an empty basket. This final object is modest, but it marks the end of the sequence. The wheel remains there, ready for work that is not described. To add another episode of spinning after the return would be to invent one. The account closes instead with the basket set beside the wheel. At the beginning the courtyard was a workplace in which thread was finished; at the end it is the destination of a return and the setting for putting things away. The place repeats while the activity changes.

Domestic labor often moves through spaces that a formal record would keep apart: a shop for exchange, a fountain for water, a relative's room for help with a meal. The spinner's time is not divided into a single occupation followed by a single leisure period. Her agreed price and her aunt's meal preparation are part of the same day, connected by walking. The story gives a sequence and one duration for a visit; it offers no clock for the other passages. That lack does not prevent the route from being reconstructed. It asks only that the unmeasured parts remain unmeasured and that the spinner, rather than every person in the surrounding places, remain the subject of the chain.

The spinner's errands are held together by hands that keep changing what they carry. Thread goes out toward the weaver, water comes away from the fountain, and an empty basket returns to the courtyard. None is a valuable load in the manner of stone or timber, but each requires attention. Water can spill before it reaches the aunt's house; thread can tangle before a price is agreed. The hour spent helping with a meal is not paid in the account, yet it belongs to the obligations of kin as firmly as the visit to the shop belongs to trade. At the end, the courtyard contains the wheel and the basket again, though not the thread in its earlier form. A reader following only objects might mistake this for several unrelated tasks. A reader following the person sees one day in which work, exchange, water, and family help are joined by a series of ordinary walks.

title: 夜间巡守
text:
A wall at night is a working place, not merely a boundary drawn around a town. Doors have to be checked, lamps tended, and unexpected traffic questioned. The guardroom keeps the key and provides a place to light a lantern before anyone sets out. The tower offers a view, but the practical concern in this account is its door. The river post is more exposed. A boatman arriving late is not necessarily dangerous, yet a watchman cannot ignore a person who appears after the gates have closed. These duties produce a route shared for several hours by a watchman and his helper.

Night alters the meaning of familiar distances. A wall passage may be easy by daylight and difficult under a small flame. The north tower and river post are separate points of attention, even if they belong to one defensive circuit. An hour passes before the move to the river post, but the narrative does not say that the walk along the wall consumes that hour. Later there is another hour of tending the lantern at the post. These spans of time belong to the order and duration of work. The only measured travel is a ride of fifteen minutes toward the south gate.

At the closing of the gates, Dario the watchman and his helper Pino light a lantern in the guardroom. They walk to the north tower and inspect its door. An hour later they go along the wall to the river post, where they question a late boatman. Near midnight Dario rides a horse to the south gate, a trip of fifteen minutes, and reports the encounter to the captain. Pino remains at the river post to tend the lantern for another hour. At dawn he walks alone to the guardroom and returns the key.

The separation at the river post is decisive. The watchman rides to report the encounter to the captain, while the helper stays behind with the lantern. A reader could easily send both men to the south gate because they have been named together throughout the earlier route. The words do not permit it. The helper's next journey is at dawn, when he walks alone back to the guardroom and returns the key. The captain is not given a route; he is a recipient of the report. The boatman is questioned at the river post but is not followed into a separate chain by this account.

The pattern of watch work includes motion and stillness. Inspecting a door requires reaching it; questioning a boatman requires remaining at the post long enough to learn why he is there. Tending a lantern is no less part of the route because it happens without a change of place. The helper's return to the guardroom completes the sequence that began with lighting the same lantern. The watchman's line ends at the south gate, where the report is delivered. Neither line supplies an invented return for the other person. Such limits are as important as the stops themselves when a shared nocturnal errand becomes two different itineraries.

The lantern is the most visible object in the watchmen's story, though it does not travel to every final destination. It begins in the guardroom, passes the tower, and reaches the river post with the two men. When their paths divide, its tending remains the helper's business. The watchman's report goes instead toward the captain at the south gate. A key then makes the helper's dawn return necessary. These objects anchor the order of the night without creating activities for everyone who sees them. The boatman is questioned but does not become a companion on the wall. The captain receives a report but has no stated outward journey. The watch can be imagined as a ring around the town, yet this account gives only two partial lines: a shared stretch, one ride away, and one later walk back. Their incompleteness is a feature of the testimony, not a defect to be filled with a guessed patrol.

title: 陶工父女
text:
A potter's workshop is crowded with shapes that are not yet strong enough to be used. Bowls must be lifted without pressing a thumb into their rims. The kiln yard takes the fragile pieces out of the workroom, but arranging them for firing is only one part of the process. Water is needed for the work and for the people doing it; a nearby well is therefore a real stop, not an ornament in the landscape. The painter's room lies elsewhere. Blue pigment collected there will matter to later decoration, although no painting is described in this account. These places form a small circuit of production whose order cannot be changed at will.

Father and daughter work together at first. The younger person is thirteen, but her age does not tell us that she performs only easy tasks. She helps shape bowls, assists with the move to the kiln yard, and draws water. The donkey carries the bowls, while the people lead it. The difference matters: a loaded animal does not prove that either worker rode. After the well the tasks diverge. The father returns to watch the firing; the daughter seeks pigment and eventually brings it back to the workshop. Their names remain connected by the pottery, not by an uninterrupted shared route.

Rosa, a potter's daughter of thirteen, helps her father Alessio shape bowls at the workshop in the morning. They lead a donkey carrying the bowls to the kiln yard, where they arrange the pieces for firing. After the fire is lit, the two walk to the nearby well and draw water. Alessio then returns to the kiln yard to watch the firing for three hours. Rosa instead walks to the painter's room to collect blue pigment. Before dusk she brings the pigment back to the workshop, a walk of ten minutes.

The firing occupies three hours at the kiln yard. That period is the father's attendance to a process in one place, not the time required to return from the well. The daughter's final walk to the workshop takes ten minutes. Nothing says that her earlier journey to the painter's room took the same length, even if the two places were close. The exact measure belongs where the words put it. The well visit is shared, the kiln return belongs to the father, and the pigment errand belongs to the daughter.

The workshop appears twice in the daughter's line. It is first a place where bowls are shaped and later a place to which a new material is brought. The return does not erase the intervening stops or turn her father's kiln watch into one of her activities. The father does not have a stated trip to the painter's room. Such distinctions can be hidden when a household's work is narrated collectively. A potter may speak of 'our bowls' and 'our kiln,' but individual hands go in different directions once the shared morning is over. The chain preserves both the cooperation and the division without requiring a guessed account of everything each person did after dusk.

The bowls move while they are fragile, and the pigment moves after the daughter's route has separated from her father's. Neither object is decoration in the account. A bowl broken on the way to the kiln cannot be repaired by a later fine color; pigment brought to an empty workshop cannot stand in for a watched firing. The three-hour watch binds the father to heat and uncertainty at one place. The daughter, who helped begin the work, attends to what the bowls may need after they have survived. Her walk back to the workshop gives her line a return that his line does not have. The well falls between these tasks, a shared stop whose water will serve both people. This ordinary division of labor makes a household look less like a single worker and more like a set of overlapping routes, each complete only as far as the account follows it.

title: 渡河的奶酪商
text:
The ferry landing is both a place of trade and a point at which the seller's usual ground ends. Cheese can be sold from a stall while the seller remains beside the water, but fresh stock has to be obtained from a farm across it. The ferry makes the crossing possible without requiring the seller to own a boat. A basket can be carried aboard, held steady, and unloaded on the far bank. These small actions keep the cheese from being crushed or wetted. The farm lies beyond the bank, not at the moment of disembarkation. Buying there has a different purpose from unloading at the river's edge. A roadside shrine introduces another brief stop before the return.

The stall itself is not simply the start of the journey. Wrapping three wheels for a customer is a sale-related task before departure. On the far side the seller buys cheese and takes bread, a modest pause at the same farm. Later he leaves a coin at a shrine. Such a gesture has no obvious place in an inventory of cheese, yet it is part of the route as told. The ferry returns him to the landing in the afternoon, and the new stock is weighed at the stall. The place repeats at the end under a different activity.

Gino the cheese seller opens his stall by the ferry landing and wraps three wheels for a customer. He boards the ferry with a basket, crosses to the far bank in ten minutes, and unloads the basket. At a farm beyond the bank he buys fresh cheese and eats a piece of bread. Gino then walks to a roadside shrine and leaves a coin there. In the afternoon he takes the ferry back to the landing and weighs the new cheese at his stall.

One crossing has a stated duration of ten minutes. The return is also made by ferry, but the narrative gives it no separate number. It would be tempting to copy the ten minutes to the return because the same stretch of water is crossed. A current, a wait for the boat, or a different landing could change the experience; more simply, the account does not measure it. The walk to the shrine is explicit, while the passage from the far bank to the farm is given only by the farm's location beyond the bank. A route can still connect these stops without pretending to know each missing detail.

The objects of the journey are as important as the names of its places. The first wheels are prepared for a customer. The basket crosses empty enough to receive stock, and the newly bought cheese comes back to be weighed. The coin left at the shrine is not payment for the cheese. By attending to what happens at each stop, the account avoids treating every movement as a delivery and every named location as a shop. The stall, bank, farm, shrine, and stall again make a loop whose order explains why the seller took the ferry at all.

The cheese seller's basket is unloaded at the far bank before the purchase at the farm. That small separation prevents the bank from becoming merely another name for the farm. The shrine also has its own action, slight in time and weight but distinct from buying and selling. A coin is left there rather than exchanged for food. The return ferry restores the seller to a familiar landing, but the goods now have a different status: they must be weighed and offered. The water between the banks remains the same obstacle on both crossings, while the account measures only the outward one. Trade often leaves such uneven traces. A price might be remembered, a crossing timed because it was unusually quick, and a short walk described without numbers. The day can still be read in order if the known acts are kept at their own places.

title: 木匠与学徒
text:
A carpenter's workshop is a place of repair as much as invention. A table may have lost a leg, warped in damp weather, or simply ceased to fit the room for which it was made. Once repaired, it still has to be carried to its owner and set where it can be used. The cart gives the two workers a way to move a piece too awkward for one pair of hands. A timber yard offers material for the next order, but choosing planks there is not the same task as fitting the finished table in a merchant's house. The day links present work to future work without allowing either to stand in for the other.

The apprentice shares the first stages of the route. He helps repair the table, carries it, and looks over the planks. The guild hall and the school stand for different claims on the afternoon. The master owes a fee at one; the apprentice practices figures at the other. Schooling is not outside the craft merely because it occurs away from the workshop. Measuring a board and keeping an account both require numbers. Yet the account of the day states only the lesson and its length, not a future use for it. The workshop receives the apprentice again when he returns to sweep away shavings.

A carpenter named Renzo and his apprentice Milo repair a table in their workshop just after sunrise. They carry the finished table by cart to a merchant's house and fit it beside the hearth. From there they walk to the timber yard to choose planks for another order. At noon Renzo takes the cart to the carpenter guild hall, where he pays a fee. Milo instead walks to a small school and practices figures for an hour. Afterward he goes on foot to the workshop and sweeps away the shavings.

The shared route ends at the timber yard. After that the master takes the cart to the guild hall, while the apprentice walks to the school. The cart's earlier presence does not follow the apprentice into his later errands. His lesson lasts an hour, a duration spent inside the school. The subsequent passage back to the workshop is on foot, with no measured travel time. The master's fee is paid at the hall, and no later destination for him is specified. To give him the apprentice's return would make a neat household circle at the cost of the text's actual limits.

There is a practical rhythm to the order. A table must be repaired before it can be fitted in the merchant's room. New planks can be chosen after that delivery, when the cart is no longer burdened with the finished piece. The fork in the route comes only then. Lists of trades sometimes hide the differences between master and apprentice under the same label, carpenter. Here their occupations are related, but their afternoons cannot be collapsed into one chain. Each activity is tied to a place and a purpose. The fact that both began in the workshop explains their cooperation without erasing the separate uses they make of the town later in the day.

Shavings on a workshop floor are the residue of an earlier task, but sweeping them is the apprentice's last named action, not the master's. The master's fee at the guild hall is a different obligation connected to the same craft. A guild book might record payment and omit the table, the timber yard, and the lesson; a household account might preserve the table and forget the fee. The small itinerary holds them together without pretending that both people attended each stop. The workshop begins as a place of shared repair and ends as the apprentice's destination. The merchant's room and timber yard lie between those uses of the same place. What looks like a single carpenter's day in the name of the trade is therefore two days interlocked for a while. The branch after the yard is as important as the earlier journey by cart, because it shows how training and business make different claims on the afternoon.

title: 医生沿街问诊
text:
A physician's visits are shaped by information gathered before he reaches a patient. A note read in the study may contain a description of symptoms, but a description is not an examination. Instruments have to be packed in case they are needed. A horse makes a journey between households possible in a day, though it does not determine how long a physician remains in any one room. The cloth dealer's house contains the first patient. The barber's shop supplies a different kind of expertise, a conversation about a salve rather than another examination. The monastery infirmary is yet another setting, where care is organized around people who live apart from the dealer's household.

The route takes the physician from a private study into rooms whose owners expect judgment. He may see one person for a short time and another for longer, but only the first examination is given a duration here. The streets themselves are named chiefly through the means of travel. A ride brings him to the dealer's house, another to the barber, and a later ride to the infirmary. The return by horse closes the day at the study. The account does not make the barber his patient; their meeting is a consultation about treatment. Such differences matter when every stop is to be given a label more precise than 'medical work.'

Before noon, Orlando the physician reads a note in his study and packs a small case of instruments. He rides a horse to the cloth dealer's house, where he examines the dealer's feverish son. The examination lasts half an hour. Orlando then rides to the barber's shop across the square and consults the barber about a salve. After that he rides to the monastery infirmary, a journey of twenty minutes, and visits an elderly patient. At sunset he returns by horse to his study and writes down what he has seen.

Half an hour belongs to the examination in the dealer's house. Twenty minutes belongs to the ride to the monastery infirmary. These quantities lie close together in the story, but they describe different things. The first is time spent with a patient; the second is time spent on the road. No measured duration is supplied for the earlier rides or for the return at sunset. A faithful chain can hold those empty fields without losing the order of the visits. It is the sequence of places and activities, not a complete clock, that makes the itinerary intelligible.

The final writing in the study gives the first stop a second role. At the start it was a place to read and prepare; at the end it is a place to put observations into words. That return is not another medical visit. It may be as necessary to the physician's work as carrying instruments, but it has a different location and a different action from either examination. The story also leaves the patients where they are. The cloth dealer's son and the elderly person at the infirmary are people in the account, yet no travel of their own is described. The physician's route is the one that can be reconstructed from the stated movements.

The physician's case returns to the study with him, but the account does not say that every instrument in it was used. A packed object is preparation, not proof of a procedure. Likewise, a conversation about a salve at the barber's shop is consultation rather than a visit to a third patient. These distinctions keep the route from multiplying medical acts simply because medicine is its theme. The dealer's household and the monastery offer two patients in different settings; the barber offers a colleague in discussion. Between them are rides whose duration is mostly unstated. The single twenty-minute passage to the infirmary stands beside the half-hour examination like two measurements of unlike things. The notes written at sunset put the observations into order after the travel is over. They make the study a destination with its own activity, not merely the place where the horse happens to stop.

title: 抄写员与信差
text:
An order written in a chancery acquires force by passing through several hands and rooms. Copying gives it a stable wording. Reading it aloud makes its contents known to a person in authority. Leaving a copy in an archive allows it to be found again when memory has become uncertain. The same sheet may seem to join everyone involved in one undertaking, but the people who bear it have distinct responsibilities. A scribe attends to the words; a messenger attends to their delivery. For a time those tasks place the two workers on the same route. Then the line divides, and only one carries the sealed order beyond the town.

The covered passage between residence and archive is part of a building complex, yet it still connects separate places where separate acts occur. The residence is where the order is read; the archive is where a copy is left. The chancery appears again when a date needs correction. This return belongs to the scribe, not to the messenger. The southern village lies farther away and requires an animal in the account. A mule makes the journey possible with the sealed sheet kept close. The person waiting at its end, the headman, is a recipient. Nothing in the account gives him a route of his own.

In the morning Gianna the scribe and Paolo the messenger meet in the chancery and copy a short order. Together they walk to the bishop's residence, where Gianna reads the order aloud and Paolo waits with the seal. They take the covered passage to the cathedral archive and leave a copy with its keeper. In the afternoon Gianna returns on foot to the chancery to correct a date. Paolo instead rides a mule to the southern village, a journey of one hour, and gives the sealed order to its headman.

The shared section begins with copying, proceeds to the bishop's residence, and reaches the archive. At the residence the scribe reads while the messenger waits with the seal. Their activities differ even though their location is the same. From the archive the scribe returns to correct a date. The messenger rides to deliver the order. One hour measures that ride to the village. It does not measure the scribe's return through the town, which is described as on foot but not timed. Nor does it describe how long the order remains with the headman.

Written records can make a route seem simpler than it was. A document has a beginning and an endpoint; people have errands in between. The archive copy and the corrected date belong to the making of a reliable order, while the mule journey belongs to its transmission. Keeping the two persons distinct reveals how much cooperation can occur before a branch. It also prevents a common mistake: assigning the village to everyone mentioned in connection with the order. The messenger alone is said to reach it. The scribe's visible day ends back at the chancery, with the date corrected rather than with a second delivery imagined.

The sealed order has several copies and several guardians, but its route is not a substitute for the routes of the people carrying it. The scribe can correct a date only by returning to the chancery. The messenger can deliver the order only by leaving the town for the village. Their cooperation is genuine at the residence and archive, where both are present, yet their tasks there differ as reading differs from waiting with a seal. The covered passage gives them a shared transition before the split. Once it ends, the mule belongs to the messenger's leg, and the walk back belongs to the scribe's. A record of the order alone might mention its destination without naming the correction that preceded delivery. A record of the scribe alone might end before the village. The full account allows both lines to be read together while keeping their endings apart.

title: 卖橄榄油的一日
text:
Oil is sold in measures, but it is carried in vessels that must be filled, emptied, and cleaned. A storehouse behind a home shelters the jars before they are taken to market. The market itself gives them a different use: oil is offered from a table to people who can inspect its color and bargain over its price. The donkey helps move the load, yet it also needs care during the day. A stop at the public fountain is therefore an activity in the seller's own chain, not merely a background detail about the animal. The cousin's house supplies an empty jar that may be useful for another sale. Each place changes the condition of the goods or of the means by which they are moved.

The seller's route is a loop with a small turn away from the market. The donkey is led to water, then led on foot toward the cousin's house, and later ridden back to the storehouse. These are different ways of moving with the same animal. The account does not say that the donkey is left behind while the seller visits the cousin. That matters because the final ride needs an animal still available to her. The fountain and the cousin's house are not additional markets; they answer practical needs that trading creates.

At sunrise, Luisa the oil seller fills a jar in the storehouse behind her home. She takes a donkey to the village market and sells oil from a wooden table. When the midday crowd thins, she leads the donkey to the public fountain and gives it water. Luisa then leads the donkey on foot to her cousin's house to collect an empty jar. Before evening she rides the donkey back to the storehouse, a journey of thirty minutes, and washes the jars.

The return to the storehouse takes thirty minutes and is explicitly made on the donkey. No similar time is given for the outward trip to market or for the shorter passages in town. The midday crowd supplies a cue for when the seller changes tasks, not a measured starting hour. Before evening she is back at the place where the jars were first filled, washing them for later use. The place repeats, but the activity does not. The first stop prepares oil for sale; the last restores the vessels after the day's exchange.

Such a day cannot be reduced to a purchase and a sale. It includes care for the animal, collection of a container, and cleaning after trade. These actions are not interruptions of the occupation but conditions that allow it to continue. A list of names would identify an oil seller and perhaps a cousin; a list of places would show a storehouse, market, fountain, house, and storehouse. The order and the connections turn those lists into an itinerary. They also show where information is missing. The donkey is present, but the seller's posture on it is stated only for the return; elsewhere the words distinguish taking and leading. The chain keeps that distinction rather than forcing one mode onto every edge.

A jar returned empty can be nearly as useful as one sold full, because it allows another filling without buying a new vessel. The cousin's house thus has a practical place in the oil seller's day, even though no oil changes hands there. The fountain serves the donkey rather than a customer. These stops are easily treated as pauses around the 'real' market business, but the market could not be repeated tomorrow without water, containers, and clean storage. At sunset the storehouse receives the seller and her animal again. The thirty-minute ride is the only passage whose length is supplied. The washed jars point toward another day, but the account does not follow that day. Its boundary falls after the cleaning, when the first jars and the last jars occupy the same place in different condition. Trade has made a loop through town and back to the storehouse.

title: 旅店厨房与市集
text:
An inn's evening meal begins long before anyone sits at a table. Bread must be checked, eggs counted, vegetables bought, flour collected, beans cooked, and fodder paid for if the animals in the neighboring stable are to be kept. These tasks are close enough to seem like one household duty, but they draw the innkeeper across several settings. The kitchen supplies a starting point. The market under the loggia is a place of choice and bargaining. The miller's yard holds a heavy sack that a cart can carry more conveniently than one person can. The stable has a different claim on the inn's money, and the inn itself becomes the setting for the meal served at the end.

The carter's offer matters because it changes the manner of one leg of the route. The innkeeper walks to market and returns from the miller's yard on foot, but between those actions she rides by cart. The cart journey takes twenty minutes. It would be easy to assign that number to the later walk back because it follows the flour collection in the narrative. The words distinguish them. A cook's time has another measure again: the beans occupy two hours at the kitchen hearth. The journey and the cooking are both necessary for supper, but they are not the same interval.

Early in the morning, Antonia the innkeeper checks the bread in her kitchen and counts the remaining eggs. She walks to the market under the loggia and buys vegetables for the evening meal. A carter offers a ride, and Antonia goes by cart to the miller's yard, where she collects a sack of flour. The cart journey takes twenty minutes. At noon she returns to the inn on foot and cooks a pot of beans for two hours. Near dusk she crosses to the neighboring stable to pay for fodder, then comes back to the inn and serves supper.

The final pair of stops is small and easily overlooked. Near dusk the innkeeper crosses to the stable to pay for fodder, then comes back to serve supper. She has returned to the inn before, at noon, but that earlier visit was for cooking. The same building can hold several activities separated by an outward errand. A sequence that kept only unique place names would lose the stable trip and the last return. A sequence that counted every mention of supper as a meal eaten by the innkeeper would add an activity the account does not describe.

The inn is a business whose labor is dispersed through neighboring streets. A customer may see only a hot pot and a filled bowl. The keeper sees the market purchase, the cart ride, the slow cooking, and the obligation to the stable that supports travelers and their animals. Some durations are provided, others are not. We know the cart journey's twenty minutes and the beans' two hours; we do not know how long it took to walk to market or across to the stable. This uneven record is sufficient to reconstruct a day if each action is placed where it belongs and if the unstated times are allowed to remain unstated.

Flour, vegetables, and fodder belong to the same inn but serve different recipients. The flour and vegetables enter the kitchen; the fodder answers for animals kept nearby. A guest eating supper may see none of these exchanges. The innkeeper's route gives the hidden work a shape: out to the market, by cart to the miller's yard, back to the hearth, across to the stable, and back again. The final return is only a short crossing in the words of the account, but it matters because supper is served afterward at the inn. Two hours at the pot are not two hours on the road. The cart's twenty minutes are not a measure of the market walk. When the day's activities are placed in sequence, the neighboring buildings cease to blur into one business and become distinct sites of buying, carrying, cooking, paying, and serving.

title: 绳索作坊与港口账簿
text:
Before sunrise, Cecilia, a rope maker aged twenty-three, sorts hemp with her apprentice Paolo in the rope shop. The shutter is open only at its upper edge, and the pale fibers catch what little light comes from the lane. Hemp is sold by weight, but its worth to this household depends also on length, dryness, and the amount of tangled waste concealed inside a bundle. Cecilia has inherited a customer's suspicion of unusually neat packages. Paolo knows the good fibers by their smoothness, although his hands still confuse a strong strand with one that merely looks thick. Their smallest pieces belong to household cord, not to a ship's cable.

They walk for twelve minutes to the covered ropewalk, where they twist a new cable for an hour. Its long roof is supported by posts whose bases have been darkened by wet winters. The space could hardly be mistaken for an ordinary workshop: the useful length of the ground matters as much as the quality of any tool. A crooked run puts unequal strain into the growing rope. Outside, the air smells of damp timber, while under the roof there is a dust that seems too light to settle. To Paolo the finished thickness is impressive; to Cecilia, evenness matters more than size.

The two push a handcart to the north quay and deliver the cable beside a merchant vessel. The cart has only a low rail around its wooden bed. The harbor's uneven stones make the loaded cart slow, and each wheel has a separate voice. The vessel beside them bears no grand decoration. Its importance lies in the sacks and barrels below its rail, ordinary cargo with enough value to make a defective rope an expensive embarrassment.

At midday they go on foot to the harbor kitchen and eat bread at a narrow table. The room is neither an inn nor a private household, but a place where several kinds of harbor labor have a common price for food. Their table is close enough to the door for the draught to disturb the crumbs. Cecilia's portion is paid from the cable's price; Paolo's belongs to the obligations of apprenticeship. Their shared meal does not erase that difference. Across the room, clothing distinguishes a clerk from a porter more clearly than the bread on either plate distinguishes their appetites.

After the meal Cecilia walks to the customs office and checks the payment entry for half an hour. The book lies on a desk polished unevenly by sleeves and elbows. Her cable appears in a short line between other goods, reduced to a description, a weight, and a sum. The account gives no hint of the ropewalk's length or the splintered cart wheel. Such a line is useful precisely because it leaves out most of the morning. Cecilia's concern is the figure beside her name, for a copied mistake can survive longer than any spoken promise about a later correction.

Paolo instead walks for eight minutes to the parish chapel, where he practices reading for half an hour. His lesson belongs to the same afternoon as Cecilia's account, but it takes place beyond her view. The letters on his page have the unfamiliar dignity of marks that remain still while their meanings change with another person's voice. The chapel has no schoolroom grandeur. Its bench is rough, and light from the doorway falls across only one end. Reading may someday make a bill less mysterious to him; for now, the page demands the patient attention that rope fibers already receive from his fingers.

Toward dusk Cecilia returns on foot to the rope shop and stores the unused hemp. The bundles are lighter than they were at dawn, and the empty place near the shutter measures the day's sale more clearly than a total in the harbor book. Outside this household, a cable belongs to the equipment of a ship. Inside it, the same object accounts for food, rent, an apprentice's maintenance, and a woman's claim to payment under her own name. Nothing in the lane announces those connections. The shop remains a narrow room, with work enough in its remaining fibers for another morning.

title: 铸钟人的量衡
text:
At first light, Benedetto the bell founder examines a wax pattern with Ilario, his seventeen-year-old apprentice, in the foundry. A bell begins here as a shape that cannot survive the making of its metal successor. The wax bears a saint's name, a border of leaves, and one letter that is thinner than its neighbors. None of these details makes a sound, yet the parish has paid attention to each. Ilario admires the border. Benedetto is more interested in the thickness of the curve below it, where beauty and the behavior of heated metal must come to terms before any inscription can matter.

They walk to the mold yard and inspect the clay casing for twenty minutes. The yard has a covered edge, but its center is open to the changing sky. Dryness is not the same thing as hardness, and a surface that looks sound can conceal a weakness beneath it. The casing carries the evidence of fingers, cloth, and the wooden forms that have supported it. It is an awkward object to regard as a commercial promise. To a parish committee the order concerns a bell; to the workshop it concerns the safety of a shape that must endure conditions no customer wishes to watch closely.

They take a small cart to the public scales and weigh copper beneath the stone arcade. The balance has the authority of the town behind it, an authority the founder's own weights cannot always command in a dispute. A market woman near the pillars has onions arranged in shallow heaps. Her trade and his require different sums, but both depend on a stranger's willingness to accept a measure. The copper is dull enough to disappoint anyone expecting a golden surface. Its weight matters more than its color, and the figure on the clerk's slip belongs beside the workshop's order rather than among its decorations.

Benedetto then walks to the parish tower and measures the empty bell frame. The stair is narrow, the timber above it wider and older than it appears from the street. Sound will eventually travel freely over roofs that the founder can see only in fragments through the openings. A bell that fits the written order can still prove troublesome in a frame built for an earlier casting. The parish's account contains a single commission, while the tower contains the consequences of several generations of repairs. Its mismatched beams are a quieter history than the names intended for the new metal.

Ilario goes separately on foot to the charcoal store, where he purchases two sacks. The merchant's room is black even where sunlight reaches the threshold. A sack has a shape and an apparent fullness, but little of the certainty offered by the public balance. The charcoal belongs to the unseen cost of a bell: fuel has no place in its final inscription, although the casting cannot exist without it. Ilario has permission to purchase only the stated amount. His age gives him work enough for a man's shoulders, while the master's instructions still determine the size of his credit.

At noon Ilario brings the sacks by handcart to the foundry and stacks the fuel. The corner chosen for it is dry and far from the wax, a small arrangement whose wisdom is clearer to the workshop than to a visitor. Above the bench, a rough drawing gives the bell's dimensions without its ornament. To anyone acquainted only with a bell in a tower, that mixture of fragile patterns and dirty sacks would be difficult to recognize.

In the early afternoon Benedetto returns on foot to the foundry and revises the frame drawing for an hour. The tower has supplied a correction that the parish's original measurements missed. On paper the change is a small adjustment of lines. In the agreement it would be harder to describe, since money and responsibility are less easily moved than ink. For the present, the alteration belongs to the workbench. Beyond the yard, the existing bells keep their familiar hours; this unfinished one has already occupied most of two people's day without contributing a single note to the town's common sound.

title: 书页与皮封
text:
Before the first market bell, Ottavia, a bookbinder, folds printed sheets in her workshop. The shop is too small for a press, and its chief tools have none of a printer's size or noise. Nevertheless, a stack of sheets is not yet a book that a traveler can put safely into a bag. Ottavia's bench is covered with pieces of older work. A strip cut from a damaged page has a second value here, as material whose usefulness no longer depends on the words printed across it.

She walks for a quarter of an hour to the printer's courtyard, where she collects the missing gathering. A wall on the shaded side remains cold, although the roofs above it have begun to brighten. The absent sheets are few enough to seem a trivial failure to anyone outside the trade. Inside a book, however, a gap of several pages has greater force than its small weight suggests. The paper in her parcel carries an odor different from that of the leather on her bench. Print can multiply a text, but every individual copy still has its own capacity for disorder.

From the courtyard she goes on foot to the leather stall and chooses a brown calfskin. The skin is thin enough for a modest binding and sound along the parts that must bend. Its uneven edge belongs to a living creature's shape, whereas the book requires a rectangle. The stallholder's price allows nothing for a binder's mistakes in cutting. Nearby, straps and patched shoes offer other futures for the same material. A fine cover might suggest wealth in a reader's hands; on the market board it is still one choice among goods whose surfaces carry the marks of tanning, weather, and uncertain storage.

At the third hour Ottavia returns on foot to her workshop and sews the book for two hours. Her window provides a better measure of useful light than the street's passing noise. Sewing has an outward simplicity that hides the cost of a misplaced hole. The gatherings must open without pulling apart, and the back must hold without making the volume stubborn. There is no grand decoration in this commission. A purchaser who wants a working book may notice bad movement sooner than a missing flourish. The repeated stitches give the book a strength that cannot be judged from the elegance of its title.

After midday she walks to the grammar school and delivers the bound volume. The schoolroom contains a mixture of boards, benches, and personal belongings whose arrangement offers little resemblance to the orderly page. The master's payment has been agreed in advance, but the book itself belongs among the objects that can be lent, damaged, and disputed. Ottavia recognizes her calfskin most readily by a small dark patch near its lower edge. To another eye that mark may be a defect. To hers it is a familiar feature in an object that has ceased to belong to the workshop's unfinished stock.

She then walks for ten minutes to the convent gate, where she collects a damaged psalter. This is a separate commission, not the same volume on its return. Its boards are older, its covering more tired, and its leaves less even in color. Repair offers a different kind of uncertainty from new work. The weakest part may be hidden beneath an earlier repair that looks sound enough from outside. The convent has little interest in a fashionable cover. The important qualities are durability and a familiar opening, for repeated use has given particular pages a place in the book's physical memory.

Near sunset Ottavia returns on foot to her workshop and records the repair price. The psalter lies apart from the remnants of the schoolbook, and the two commissions occupy separate lines in her small account. A day's route can join printer, leather seller, school, and convent without making their requirements alike. One wants complete sheets, another a sale, another a durable new volume, and the last a usable old one. The workshop's narrow door is common to them only through her labor. In the thinning light, scraps on the bench are less waste than a reserve against tomorrow's small necessities.

title: 市税员的一圈路
text:
At dawn Matteo, a market toll collector aged forty-two, checks the blank receipts in the gate office. The office stands close enough to the entrance for road dust to settle on its lower shelf. On a busy morning a missing receipt could become an accusation, while too many unused ones might suggest that trade has been lighter than expected. Matteo's own family has no interest in such distinctions at breakfast. The town, however, pays him to make the passage of goods leave a mark that can be counted.

He walks for six minutes to the livestock pen and records the fee on three goats. The animals have no patience for the fence, and their seller has little for the book. A goat's value depends on more than the number written beside it: age, milk, soundness, and the season belong to a bargain in ways the toll cannot accommodate. The fixed fee has the convenience of indifference. Matteo's receipt does not say whether the seller will make a profit. It says only that these animals have entered a place where the town claims a small part of their commercial possibility.

He goes on foot to the cloth arcade, where he checks a merchant's stamped receipt. A chest near the stall has iron bands whose strength seems greater than its contents require. Cloth can absorb a remarkable amount of a household's wealth without occupying much ground. The merchant's paper is creased at the corners, and its stamp is shallow on one side. A poor impression is not necessarily a false one. The arcade provides shade for goods and people alike, but it gives no easy protection against the suspicion that one trader has purchased an advantage another must pay to obtain.

Near the third hour he walks to the fish benches and enters two basket fees in the ledger. The smell is strongest beside the shaded wall, where the stones remain wet. A basket looks like an obvious unit until its contents make that certainty inconvenient. Large fish lie at angles, smaller ones fill gaps, and a cover can conceal either abundance or a disappointing bottom layer. The fee concerns the basket, while the quarrel concerns what the basket appears to promise. Matteo's book has little room for either smell or disappointment, although both belong closely to the commerce taking place around him.

At noon he walks to the communal fountain and drinks water. The water is cold against his dust-dried mouth. The lip of the basin is smooth where buckets have rubbed it, and a dark line on the stone records a height the water does not presently reach. A fountain serves trades that have no common interest elsewhere in the town. Dusty hands, stained cloth, empty jars, and tired animals all have claims on the same supply. Matteo's leather book remains under his arm. The seal that gives him authority over market goods has no useful power over the pace of a crowded basin.

Afterward he returns on foot to the gate office and totals the receipts for half an hour. The desk offers a stillness that the market has lacked. Three goats, a merchant's paper, and two fish baskets have become entries of comparable size, despite the unequal effort of collecting and checking them. The town's concern is a total with supporting marks. For Matteo, each figure retains something of a face or a voice that the arithmetic cannot use. The difference matters most when the sum fails, for a misplaced coin is easier to describe than the circumstances in which it vanished.

In the afternoon he walks for fifteen minutes to the council treasury and deposits the day's coins. The journey is short enough to belong to his ordinary duties, yet the purse makes it unlike an unburdened return home. A counted sum has a peculiar weight that cannot be measured solely in metal. At the treasury it passes into a chest with money from other gates and other days. The individual market transactions become difficult to distinguish there. Matteo's name remains on the account, attached to an amount that must agree with the receipts in the book beneath his arm.

title: 嫁妆针线的差事
text:
In the early morning Beatrice, a seamstress aged thirty-one, compares linen lengths with Agnese, a fifteen-year-old apprentice, in the family storeroom. The household's marriage chest stands open, though the wedding itself is several weeks away. Folded cloth has the appearance of completed wealth. Along an unfinished edge, however, the work still to be paid for is easy to see. Some lengths belong to the family, others have been purchased on credit, and a narrow embroidered strip has a value no one in the room would express as its weight. Beatrice's concern is whether the useful cloth matches the garments promised in the list.

They walk for ten minutes to the thread seller's stall and buy sewing thread. The morning street is bright above their heads and still shaded at their feet. Thread occupies so little space that its price can seem unreasonable beside the bulk of the linen. Yet weak thread can turn an expensive garment into an early repair. Agnese has a scrap against which to compare the color. Beatrice's chosen skein has less brightness than its neighbor.

They go on foot to the bride's chamber, where they fit a linen shift for half an hour. The room has a painted chest and a window whose curtain is patched near the bottom. Such details belong to different accounts of a family's standing. The painted wood is made for display, the curtain for use, and the shift must answer both demands in its own way. Beatrice's experience is apparent in the quiet economy of the fitting. Agnese's attention is fixed on the relation between seam and movement, something the flat linen in the storeroom could not have shown her.

Before midday Beatrice walks to the notary's room and checks the clothing list. The document gives the garments a permanence that their seams cannot share. It distinguishes a finished piece from its materials, but the terms are broad enough to leave room for an argument about quality. Beatrice is present for the clothing, not as a party to the marriage contract. Her knowledge has a practical boundary. She can recognize the shift described on the page, while the property arrangements around it belong to another profession's language and to the expectations of people whose names occupy the larger lines.

Agnese instead walks to the embroiderer's doorway and collects a finished collar. The collar is wrapped in a clean remnant, with only an edge of the stitching visible. The woman responsible for its ornament has added no material to the linen's weight that a market scale would notice. Nevertheless, the border accounts for a substantial part of its price. Agnese carries a written description of the work, but its details are easier to recognize in thread than in the list. A repeated pattern gives the piece its order; a small irregularity beside the fastening distinguishes this collar from another made to the same request.

At midday Agnese returns on foot to the family storeroom and packs the collar in the chest. The linen lengths that occupied the room earlier have not all become garments, and the chest still contains empty spaces. Packing is part of the commission, rather than a marriage ceremony or a journey to the bridegroom's house. A soft fold protects the decorated edge better than a tight roll. Within the chest, practical protection and the appearance of abundance depend on the same arrangement. The apprentice has brought back one finished piece, but the list on the shelf measures a larger obligation.

Later that afternoon Beatrice returns on foot to the family storeroom and cuts lining for an hour. The notary's list is now beside her materials, while the apprentice's collar lies inside the chest. Two errands have reached the same room by different paths. The cloth beneath Beatrice's shears is plain enough to attract little admiration, yet the garment's comfort depends on it. Marriage provides the occasion for this work without determining the order of every task. That order belongs to deliveries, available light, the readiness of other craftspeople, and the time a household can make available for a fitting.

title: 石灰窑旁的兄弟
text:
Before dawn Raffaele, a lime burner, counts empty baskets with his brother Silvio in the lime shed. Their father's years away from the district have left the household with creditors in more than one town. The shed contains little that would tempt a thief unfamiliar with the trade. Its baskets are stained, its beams rough, and the white dust along the wall has the appearance of neglect. Yet a sound basket is worth more here than a clean one. The day's materials must endure rough tracks and sharp stone before any buyer recognizes them as useful lime.

They walk uphill for twenty minutes to the quarry floor and sort pale stones for an hour. The useful pieces differ less in appearance than a stranger might expect. Some break cleanly; others include veins that will behave badly in heat. The quarry's exposed face is still cool, while a narrow strip above it has begun to catch sunlight. Their clothing is already pale at the knees. Work here has a weight that is easy to understand, but its quality depends on distinctions too small for a cartload to reveal. A large pile can conceal a disappointing proportion of unsuitable material.

They lead a pack mule to the hillside kiln and load the kiln with the selected stone. Neither brother rides the animal. Its burden belongs in the panniers, balanced against the slope rather than against a passenger's comfort. The kiln is an ordinary hollow in a built structure, made significant by its ability to contain heat without losing its own shape. Smoke stains older than either brother's present tools darken the upper stones. Good firing requires more than abundant fuel, and the loading must leave paths for heat that no finished wall will show to the mason who buys the lime.

Near midday Raffaele walks to the roadside shelter and eats bean broth. The shelter is close to the work but outside the dustiest ground. A bench and a cracked bowl offer a little comfort beside the dusty road. From the opening he can see the rising road, though the kiln is hidden behind a shoulder of earth. The food has the plain value of warmth and salt. Nothing about it belongs specifically to lime burning, except the white marks his sleeves leave on the edge of the bowl and the stubborn dryness in his mouth.

Silvio instead walks for a quarter of an hour to the builder's yard, where he delivers a sample of lime. In the family account, the brothers' earnings belong to a common purse. The sample is small enough for a folded cloth, unlike the stone that has occupied his hands all morning. At the yard, heaps of sand and broken brick offer several explanations for the color on a worker's coat. A sample carries a promise about material not yet delivered. Its modest size leaves a great deal of the eventual bargain dependent on the buyer's judgment and trust.

In the afternoon Raffaele returns on foot to the hillside kiln and tends the fire for two hours. Heat changes the meaning of distance around its mouth: a pace forward or back matters more than the view across the valley. The fuel has a market price, but waste is easier to recognize in the state of a firing than in the amount of wood remaining beside it. The work's result is meant for another craft. A wall may stand for generations without preserving the name of the person whose patient attention made its lime suitable for mortar.

Before evening Silvio walks back to the lime shed and repairs a basket. The shed is the same place where the brothers began, but the activity is different and his return is his own. Its empty spaces now correspond to material on the hill and a sample at the builder's yard. A broken rim has no place in the price of a wall, although it can delay the work supplying one. Outside, the track holds a pale trace where loaded baskets have brushed the hedge. Within the family, such small repairs belong to the continuing cost of earning anything from stone.
